d.title: Three families, and the row that matters is what each cannot do
d.caption: **An encoder cannot generate autoregressively and a decoder cannot see its own future** — and those two limits are not design preferences, they follow from the attention mask. Encoder-decoder has a dash in that row, which is why it survived for translation and summarisation: **it reads bidirectionally and writes causally.** The measured sizes are worth noting too — **T5-small is 60.5M against BERT-base's 109.5M**, so the family and the size are independent choices.

d.title: 0.3074 to the future in BERT, exactly 0.0000 in GPT-2
d.caption: The same sentence through the first head of the first layer of each. **BERT's row 2 sends 0.3074 of its weight forward and distributes across all eight positions; GPT-2's row 2 is `[0.477, 0.139, 0.384, 0.000, 0.000, 0.000]` — three exact zeros.** Which makes the architectural claim concrete and checkable: **the difference between the two families is visible in one attention row, and the zeros are exact rather than small** because of 4.5's `-inf` fill.
vars: max weight on a future token

d.title: Eighty, ten and ten — a split that exists to prevent train-serve skew
d.caption: **Fine-tuning and inference never contain `[MASK]`, so if 100% of masked positions carried it, the pretraining and downstream distributions would differ at every position the model cared about** — a built-in train-serve skew of exactly 3.5's kind, designed out of the objective. And the measured fills show the objective working: **`floor` at 0.314 for the mat position, while the subject position is a flat `girl 0.069, man 0.067, dog 0.056`** — the context constrains one far more than the other.

d.title: One mask gives Paris; three masks give “in le ##y”
d.caption: **With one mask BERT is excellent — `paris` at 0.417. With three it produces `in le ##y`, because every masked position is predicted independently and in parallel, with no access to what the others decided.** Which is the precise reason an encoder cannot generate: **generation requires each token to condition on the previous one, and MLM's parallelism is exactly the absence of that.** Not a quality problem — a structural one.

d.title: Five positions, five distributions, one forward pass
d.caption: **`logits` is (1, 5, 50257): one next-token distribution per position, all from a single pass** — this is 4.5's parallel training made concrete. **Each position is scored against the token that actually followed it, and the causal mask is what makes computing them simultaneously legitimate.** Read the confidences: **0.454 after `on` and 0.076 after `the`**, so the model is far surer about a preposition's object than about what the object is.

d.title: One model, three tasks, and the task name is in the input string
d.caption: `t5-small` translates, summarises and judges grammatical acceptability — **and the only thing that changes is the prefix.** Which is what “everything is text-to-text” means operationally: **there is no task head, no label space and no output layer per task, so adding a task means writing a prefix.** The pretraining objective matches: **span corruption drops contiguous spans and trains the decoder to emit them, and crucially a span can be any length** — which is what BERT's fixed one-token-per-mask cannot do.

d.title: 1.87x at twenty tokens and 3.46x at sixty — the gain grows with length
d.caption: **Without a cache you recompute K and V for the whole prefix at every step; with one you compute them for the new token only and append.** So the saving is quadratic in the number of generated tokens, which the two measurements show directly: **0.52s against 0.98s at 20 tokens, and 1.31s against 4.52s at 60.** Which means **the cache is not an optimisation you benchmark once — its value depends on how much you generate**, and at a thousand tokens it is the difference between usable and not.

d.title: 10.74 GB of cache for one sequence, or 0.17 with MQA
d.caption: LLaMA-2-70B at 4096 tokens in fp16: **10.74 GB with full multi-head attention, 1.34 GB with GQA8, 0.17 GB with MQA** — an 8× and 64× reduction from sharing K and V heads, reproducing the reference exactly. Then the scaling table is the number that governs serving: **at 32k context and batch 32, GQA8 still needs 343.6 GB, and at 128k with batch 128 it is 5,497.6 GB.** **The cache, not the weights, is what makes long context expensive.**

d.title: The partial result is wrong, and the rescaling makes it exact
d.caption: **After the first block the running output is −0.7038, which is *wrong* — a partial result normalised by a partial denominator.** The second block raises the running max from −0.1746 to 0.1312, **rescales what was already accumulated by `exp(m − m_new)`, adds its own contribution, and lands on 0.330191 — exactly what standard attention gives.** Nothing is discarded or approximated, which is why **block size does not affect accuracy: max absolute difference stays at ~1.5e-07 from block size 1 to 100.**

d.title: Four O(n) patterns, and they get there four different ways
d.caption: **Longformer and BigBird keep real attention and restrict *which* pairs are computed — window plus a few global tokens, with BigBird adding random connections and the proof that sparse attention is Turing complete.** Linformer and Performer instead **approximate**: one projects K and V to a fixed dimension before attending, the other uses random feature maps to approximate the softmax kernel without ever forming the matrix. **Which is the real split: restricted-exact against full-approximate.**

d.title: Verification is parallel even though generation is not
d.caption: **Decoding is sequential because token `t+1` needs token `t`** — and speculative decoding attacks the dependency rather than the cost: **a small draft model proposes `K` tokens cheaply, and the large model verifies all `K` in a single forward pass.** The asymmetry is the whole trick: **scoring a given sequence is one parallel pass, while producing it was `K` sequential ones.** And because rejected tokens are discarded, **the output distribution is unchanged — this is lossless.**

nodes.label: A small draft proposes K tokens
The target verifies all K at once
So the output distribution is unchanged

d.title: Every configuration was slower than plain greedy decoding
d.caption: **Plain greedy on gpt2-medium took 4.85s. The best speculative configuration took 9.60s — twice as slow.** And the mechanism worked exactly as advertised: **tokens per target pass rose from 1.71 to 3.47 as `K` grew.** The reason it still lost is the draft: **gpt2 is 124M against gpt2-medium's 355M, so the draft costs about a third of the target per pass, and acceptance fell from 61% to 32% as `K` grew.** A 2.9× ratio is nowhere near enough.

d.title: At 90% acceptance K=8 gives 6.13 tokens a pass; at 30% it gives 1.43
d.caption: **The expected gain saturates in `K` and is governed almost entirely by the acceptance rate `a`: at `a = 0.3`, raising `K` from 1 to 8 moves 1.30 to 1.43 — nothing.** Which explains §02's result and dictates the production shape: **pair a 7B target with a 1B draft, or train a draft specifically to imitate the target.** Checked at one position, the two models disagreed outright — **gpt2-medium wanted ` 1950` and gpt2 wanted ` late`.**

d.title: Four bytes to half a byte, and 280 GB to 35
d.caption: The arithmetic is simply bytes per parameter, and it reproduces the reference exactly — **but the row that changes what is possible is INT4: a 70B model at 35 GB fits on one 40GB card, where at FP16 it needs 140.** The four named methods differ in how they protect accuracy: **GPTQ uses second-order information one-shot, AWQ protects the small fraction of weights that matter most to activations, GGUF targets CPU and Apple Silicon, and QLoRA quantises the frozen base to 4-bit and trains adapters above it.**

d.title: Five of seven techniques are lossless, so the order is not a trade-off question
d.caption: Read the “lossy” column: **the KV cache, FlashAttention, continuous batching and PagedAttention all recover pure waste — recomputation, memory traffic, idle slots, over-allocation — so they are not trades and should be done first.** GQA is slightly lossy for an 8× cache reduction. **Quantisation costs 0.5–2% accuracy, and speculative decoding costs nothing but only works with a much cheaper draft** — which §02 measured the hard way.

d.title: Twenty tokens per parameter, and the models that ignored it
d.caption: **Because `N ∝ C^0.5` and `D ∝ C^0.5`, their ratio is constant — the rule is simply *scale parameters and data together*, at about 20 tokens per parameter.** The table is the finding: **Chinchilla at 70B/1400B used less compute than Gopher at 280B/300B and beat it**, because Gopher spent 1.1 tokens per parameter. And **LLaMA-3 8B is at 1875 — a long way past optimal in the other direction**, which §02 explains. Via `C ≈ 6ND`, **a compute budget gives you a model size and a token count in one line.**

d.title: Gopher was 18.7x short of its own optimal token count
d.caption: The shortfall column is the Chinchilla paper's argument in one number: **Gopher should have seen 5,600B tokens and saw 300B.** But the modern models at the bottom are not correcting toward 20 — **they are overshooting it deliberately, because Chinchilla optimises training compute only.** If you serve a model at volume, **overshoot `D` and shrink `N`: a one-off training cost against a permanent inference saving** — which is why LLaMA-3 8B sits at 1875 tokens per parameter rather than 20.

d.title: Each 10x in parameters buys less than the last, and the law predicts how much
d.caption: With Kaplan's constants the drops shrink monotonically: **0.6447 from 1e6 to 1e7, and 0.2688 from 1e11 to 1e12.** The practical value is not the curve but the extrapolation: **fit it on small models you can afford, and know roughly what a run 100× larger will achieve before committing to it.** Which is what **turned large-model training from a gamble into a budgeting exercise** — and note `L_inf = 1.69`, an irreducible floor the law says no amount of scale removes.

d.title: A claim worth testing, because of what follows if it is true
d.caption: **The standard account: few-shot learning appears around 1B, code generation around 10B, chain-of-thought around 100B — performance at chance across orders of magnitude, then a sharp rise.** If true the implications are serious: **you cannot predict what a larger model will do, and safety-relevant capabilities could appear without warning.** Which is exactly why it is worth testing rather than repeating — **and §06's conclusion is to re-score with a continuous metric first, because most reported cliffs are `p^k` in disguise.**

nodes.label: At chance, then a sharp rise
If true: larger models are unpredictable
So test it rather than repeat it

d.title: Four uses, and two of them contradict the headline result
d.caption: **Fit before you commit: train a ladder of small models, fit the power law, extrapolate — knowing the loss a 100× run will reach is worth far more than the cost of the ladder.** `C ≈ 6ND` turns GPU-hours into a feasible `(N, D)` pair. Then the two caveats: **Chinchilla optimises training only, so serving at volume means overshooting `D` and shrinking `N`** — and **distrust sharp curves: re-score with a continuous metric before believing a capability appeared.**
